**Yes—one primary study reported an association.**

**Primary article:**  
Hikida T, et al. “Nociceptin/orphanin FQ receptor gene variation is associated with smoking status in Japanese.” *Pharmacogenomics*. 2016. PMID: [27491383](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27491383/). (Search result: `call_rlR6trYH2rBD81x9quoCYotg`.)

**Abstract:**  
“AIM: The endogenous opioid system has been reportedly implicated in tobacco/nicotine dependence. MATERIALS & METHODS: We examined the genetic effects of eight SNPs in opioid receptor-related genes on smoking status and smoking-related traits in Japanese. RESULTS: The genotypic and allelic variations of the rs2229205 SNP in the OPRL1 gene were significantly associated with smoking status, but no significant differences were found in the genetic variations of any of the SNPs with regard to smoking-related traits. The rs2229205 SNP did not show high linkage disequilibrium with the other SNPs in the linkage disequilibrium block that contained the SNP. CONCLUSION: The rs2229205 SNP in the OPRL1 gene may be a genetic factor that contributes to individual differences in the vulnerability to smoking in Japanese individuals.”

Thus, the article reports an association between **OPRL1 rs2229205** and smoking status in Japanese participants. The retrieved abstract does not provide the association’s direction, effect size, or sample size.

The available abstract reports a significant genotypic and allelic association for **OPRL1 rs2229205** with smoking status in Japanese participants, but gives no effect size, direction, sample size, or p-value. It also reports no significant association for the tested variants with smoking-related traits. I’ll record this bounded finding and its citation before answering.

The study did not find significant associations between the tested variants and smoking-related traits.
